newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia imports rise not seen as a concern.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia imports rise not seen as a concern.

text.p: News that Australia's import bill had risen for the fourth successive month had little impact on a market more focussed on Christmas, but did carry some positive news on the outlook for 1997, economists said on Wednesday.
Official data showed merchandise imports rose 1.2 percent in November, seasonally adjusted, spot on the median market forecast.
While the imports bill has risen for the last four months, it is still below the levels of early 1996 and was not pointing to a blowout of Australia's trade balance.
In fact, imports have basically been tracking sideways for much of 1997, economists said. However, the data did show some signs that activity might pick up in 1997.
"There are glimmers of light in the economy," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
Combined with recent jobs and housing data, it suggested a "gentle recovery" was underway, but he added that further data was required to determine if the recovery had a firm foundation.
The breakdown of the overall imports rise was favourable, with consumer goods up 1.9 percent, capital goods up 6.2 percent and intermediate goods posting a 1.3 percent fall.
The rise in consumer goods was seen by some economists as a sign of some growing confidence on the part of retailers.

"November is getting a bit late for consumer good imports for Christmas, so the fact that we got decent consumer good imports in November says to me that probably retailers are feeling a bit more confident about the first part of 1997," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.

Capital goods, boosted by the inclusion of two aircraft, needed a reasonably large rise, after a 7.2 percent fall in October, to allay concerns about investment targets not being met, economists said.
While there were still some concerns about capital goods, given the recent softness in the series, economists said there were signals the series would pick up in 1997.
"In underlying terms, capital goods imports are showing some signs of a recovery following a very poor start to the year," Commonwealth Bank economists said.
As Australia imports a lot of its capital goods, strength in this series was seen by economists as a sign of strong business investment, which in turn is a positive for economic growth.
While total imports have risen for the past four months, the rise has only been gradual with the largest monthly change the 1.3 percent rise in October.
As a result, financial markets were not fearing a sudden widening in the current account deficit, although there is an expectation it will widen in 1997.
"There is clearly no import boom going on, so the current account deficit will remain under control," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
After the release of the imports, forecasts for the November current account deficit ranged from A$1.6 to A$1.9 billion. The current account data is due to be released on January 6.
